Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Navy Officer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crowding: Crowded places, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others

Vignette:
Ethan, a 34-year-old Navy Officer, had always prided himself on his resilience, but the memory of the hurricane still felt like a raw wound, even two years later. He had been on shore leave in a small, bustling port town when the storm hit with unexpected ferocity. The initial chaos of the wind and rain quickly escalated as the storm surge engulfed the streets. Ethan, along with dozens of others, had been swept into a half-collapsed building, eventually finding refuge in a dark, cramped basement. They were packed shoulder-to-shoulder, water rising steadily, the air thick with the smell of ruptured liquor stores and damp earth. He remembered being pressed against a cold, grimy wall, his body contorted into an excruciating position for what felt like an eternity, the terror a cold knot in his stomach. When memories of that night came to mind now, he often found himself involuntarily tensing, his muscles aching as if his body were once again locked in that same agonizing, cramped position. The sheer extremity of the event often made him question if it had truly happened to him, as if the images flashing through his mind were from a movie rather than his own life.

In the months that followed, Ethan found his world shrinking. The once vibrant images of his life were now overshadowed by the vivid, mostly visual memories of the storm: the swirling debris, the terrified faces, the dark water rising. He had come to believe that he deserved to suffer because of what had happened, a self-imposed penance that colored every thought. This conviction made it difficult to engage with others. He started actively avoiding seeing his friends, finding their casual laughter and easy camaraderie jarring, almost offensive, against the backdrop of his internal misery. He was certain they wouldn't understand, and that he no longer belonged in their easy world.

His life as a Navy Officer, once a source of pride and structure, had become a minefield. Crowded places, like the mess hall or the gangway during watch changes, would send a jolt of panic through him, the press of bodies too reminiscent of the trapped, confined space of that basement. Specific physical locations on his ship, particularly the lower decks or any dark, enclosed compartments, could trigger a sudden, visceral fear, leaving him breathless. He would go out of his way to avoid being in the dark, often leaving lights on in his cabin or taking longer, circuitous routes to avoid unlit passages. Even the smell of alcohol, whether from a spilled drink at a social gathering or a cleaning product, could instantly transport him back to the suffocating basement, filling him with dread.

Over time, these avoidance behaviours began to take their toll. His wife, concerned by his increasing withdrawal, noticed how he would grow quiet and distant when she suggested going out with friends. He started declining invitations for social events on base, preferring to stay in his cabin, feeling isolated and set apart from his peers. He had come to the painful conclusion that he no longer belonged anywhere, neither among the cheerful civilians nor the seemingly unaffected military personnel. He knew he used to be a happy person, full of life and optimism, but now he was always miserable, a constant ache he couldn't shake. He wondered if this was simply his new reality, a permanent scar from the storm. The thought of living like this forever, trapped in a cycle of fear and self-punishment, was what finally propelled him to seek help, a desperate hope that perhaps, just perhaps, there was a way back to the person he used to be.
